titre: Snowball, the Cockatoo Who Follows the Tempo
accroche: In 2009, a cockatoo made famous on the Internet serves as a test of a hypothesis: one would synchronize to a rhythm only if one can imitate sounds.
contenu_vulgarise:
In August 2007, a bird sanctuary in South Carolina takes in a male cockatoo whose former owner claims he bobs his head in time to “Everybody (Backstreet's Back)” by the Backstreet Boys. The sanctuary's director, Irena Schulz, checks it and posts a video that goes viral. In 2008, the bird, named Snowball, arrives before two researchers at the Neurosciences Institute in La Jolla, California, Aniruddh Patel and John Iversen. For them, the idea is improbable: synchronizing to a beat was thought to be a trait almost unique to humans.

## The tempo test

A video proves nothing: the bird could be imitating the gestures of the people present, or following a rhythm that is not the music's. Between January and May 2008, Patel has Snowball play his favorite piece at several tempos and films his movements to analyze them later. The article published in 2009 in Current Biology reports that the animal, a sulphur-crested cockatoo of the subspecies eleonora, spontaneously adjusts the rhythm of his movements to the tempo of the piece to stay in sync, over a wide range of tempos. According to the first presentation of the results, in 2008, this adjustment remains limited in scope.

## A hypothesis about the origin of rhythm

The authors were not looking for a circus act. They were testing the so-called “vocal learning and rhythmic synchronization” hypothesis: synchronization to a tempo would rest on the neural circuits for complex vocal learning, which closely link hearing and the control of movement. It predicts that only species able to learn to imitate sounds (humans, certain birds, certain cetaceans and pinnipeds, but not nonhuman primates) can synchronize to a tempo.

The same year, Adena Schachner and her colleagues tested it differently. They showed that two parrots, including Snowball according to reports, line up with the music, then analyzed a worldwide video database covering hundreds of species, able to imitate sounds or not. Despite a larger number of non-imitating species and a comparable exposure of the two groups to humans and music, only the imitating species show signs of synchronization.

## What this shifts

The sense of rhythm would therefore not be a musical talent unique to humans, nor tied to our kinship with primates, but the by-product of another ability: imitating sounds. This is only a hypothesis, resting on few birds and on videos rather than controlled measurements. Its strength is that it is sharp, and therefore refutable: a single nonhuman primate that locked onto a tempo would prove it wrong.

repere.texte: According to the journal Current Biology (2009), a sulphur-crested cockatoo spontaneously adjusts the tempo of his movements to that of a piece of music, which contradicts the idea that synchronization to a beat is unique to humans.
repere.source: Patel et al., “Experimental evidence for synchronization to a musical beat in a nonhuman animal,” Current Biology, 2009

carte.punch: A cockatoo adjusts his movements to the tempo of music. Rhythm would not be unique to humans.
carte.idee: In 2009, researchers show that Snowball, a cockatoo, adjusts his movements to the tempo of a piece. A hypothesis ties this gift to vocal learning: only animals able to imitate sounds would synchronize to it.

quiz.question: What does the vocal learning hypothesis predict about synchronization to a tempo?
choix: That all species with large brains, including chimpanzees, can synchronize to it
That only humans are capable of it, because they are the only ones who make music
That only species able to imitate sounds can synchronize to it
That only young animals show it, before losing this ability
quiz.explication: The hypothesis ties synchronization to the circuits for vocal learning: it predicts that it exists in sound imitators (humans, certain birds, cetaceans, pinnipeds) and not in nonhuman primates. It therefore does not rule out all animals, does not reserve synchronization to humans, and does not depend on age.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the cockatoo Snowball come to a sanctuary in 2007?
choix: He was captured in the wild by researchers from the Neurosciences Institute
His former owner entrusted him to the sanctuary, claiming he moved in time to the beat
He was bought by Irena Schulz at an auction
He was transferred from a zoo that had just closed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Snowball's former owner entrusted the bird to the sanctuary, claiming he bobbed his head in time to a Backstreet Boys song, which the sanctuary's director then filmed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Aniruddh Patel do between January and May 2008 to test Snowball's synchronization?
choix: He measured his brain activity with electrodes
He compared Snowball to chimpanzees in a single protocol
He had his favorite piece played at several tempos and filmed his movements
He recorded his calls to compare them with those of other cockatoos
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Between January and May 2008, Patel had Snowball play his favorite piece at several tempos and filmed his movements to check whether he adjusted his rhythm to that of the music.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Adena Schachner and her colleagues show by examining a database of videos of hundreds of species?
choix: That all the species tested synchronized in the same way
That synchronization depended on the size of the animal's brain
That only songbirds, among all the species, synchronized
That only species able to imitate sounds showed signs of synchronization
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Schachner and her colleagues compared hundreds of species in a video database: despite a larger number of non-imitating species, only species able to imitate sounds showed signs of synchronization.
